title: Gut Health: What the Evidence Actually Says
hook: Wellness marketing says your gut is 'broken' and a supplement will fix it. Here's what the evidence really supports — and what's just hype.
key_points: Your gut hosts trillions of microbes that help with digestion, immunity, and more.
The best-supported way to feed a healthy microbiome is everyday diet: plenty of fiber and a variety of plants.
Fermented foods like yogurt, kefir, and kimchi can add helpful microbes.
Most marketed 'gut health' tests and many probiotic supplements aren't well backed by evidence.
There's no quick 'reset' — the microbiome shifts with consistent habits over time.
content_html: The gut microbiome — the trillions of bacteria and other microbes living in your digestive tract — has become a wellness obsession. Influencers warn that yours is "broken," and marketers sell tests and supplements promising to fix it. NPR sorted the evidence from the hype.
extra_html:
Those microbes really do matter: they help break down food, train the immune system, and produce useful compounds. But the things that actually shape them are unglamorous. The strongest evidence points to diet — eating plenty of fiber and a wide variety of plants, which feed beneficial microbes, plus fermented foods like yogurt, kefir, and kimchi that can add helpful ones.

What the evidence does not support is most of what's being sold. Consumer "gut health" tests and many probiotic supplements aren't well backed, and there's no quick "reset" — the microbiome changes gradually with consistent habits, not overnight. Antibiotics can disrupt it, which is one more reason to take them only when a doctor says they're truly needed. The reassuring takeaway: a varied, fiber-rich diet does more for your gut than anything you can buy in a bottle.

related.title: Building a Balanced Plate
related.hook: Forget counting every calorie — the simplest healthy-eating tool is a picture of a plate: half produce, a quarter grains, a quarter protein.

related.title: Why Cutting Out All Sugar Can Backfire
related.hook: Cutting added sugar is good advice — but a mouse study suggests going to the extreme and eliminating it entirely may do more harm than good, pointing to balance over zero.

related.title: Ultra-Processed Foods: The New Tobacco?
related.hook: Researchers argue ultra-processed foods echo the tobacco industry's playbook in how they're engineered and marketed — concern crosses party lines, but policy has lagged behind.

related.title: A Daily Fiber Supplement Eased Knee Arthritis Pain
related.hook: In a six-week trial, a spoonful of chicory-root fiber cut knee osteoarthritis pain about as well as physiotherapy — and people actually stuck with it. Only 3.6% dropped out, versus 21%.

flashcards.prompt: What does the evidence say is the best way to support a healthy gut microbiome?
flashcards.back_html: Everyday diet — plenty of fiber and a wide variety of plants, plus fermented foods like yogurt, kefir, or kimchi. Not a pricey test or a quick-fix supplement.

flashcards.prompt: Which of these most reliably helps your gut microbiome?

choices.text: A diet rich in fiber and varied plants

flashcards.explanation_html: Fiber and plant variety consistently feed beneficial microbes. There's no evidence for a one-time 'reset,' and fermented foods help rather than harm.
